Juan Pérez de Pineda
hwahn pā'reth dā pē-nā'da
n. (Juan Pérez de Pineda, c. 1500–1566, Sevillian exile at Geneva, translator of the Spanish New Testament and Psalms)
Spanish Juan, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Pérez, son of Pedro; de Pineda, of the pine-wood.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Juan Pérez de Pineda had been rector of the College of Doctrine at Seville and an imperial agent at Rome before the Holy Office began to move against the Sevillian evangelicals; he escaped to Geneva about 1555 and became the minister of the Spanish congregation there. From Geneva he printed what the men at home needed most: a Spanish New Testament in 1556, the Psalms in 1557, a catechism, and a Spanish version of Juan de Valdés on Romans and First Corinthians. The books went into Spain in casks and bales by the hands of Julián Hernández, and they were the immediate occasion of the Seville and Valladolid prosecutions. He died at Paris in 1566 and left his estate for the printing of a Spanish Bible — the legacy that helped carry Casiodoro de Reina's work to the press at Basel three years later. Few men have left a will that bore fruit so exactly. “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms, and a legacy as a bequest, a particular thing given by last will.

expand to see more

PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; sometimes applied to a psalm-book.

LEG'ACY, n. A bequest; a particular thing, or certain sum of money, given by last will.

CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.

SIM'PLE, a. Artless; unaffected; undesigning; sincere; weak in intellect; not wise.

Key Scripture

Psa 19:7 — "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple."

Psa 1:2 — "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."

Luk 24:32 — "And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?"

Modern Corruption

The Geneva printer-pastor whose will paid for the Bible of the Bear.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suggestion, made by both devout and sceptical writers, that the Geneva exiles provoked the Spanish persecutions and so bear some blame for the deaths at Seville. The reasoning would make every printer of Scripture responsible for the tribunal that burns its readers, and it reverses the plain moral order of the thing.

The principle to recover is that the Psalter is the church's own book of praise and complaint, and that a persecuted people needs it in its own tongue before it needs anything else but the Gospels. Pérez printed the Psalms second for that reason. “But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2) is not a counsel for scholars; it is the daily food of a man whose Bible has to be hidden in a wine cask.

Usage

"“The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7) — the Psalms he printed in 1557."

"“in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2) — food for a hidden congregation."

"“while he opened to us the scriptures?” (Luk 24:32) — a pastor to exiles in Geneva."
